mcqs.question: A medical imaging team needs to measure the exact area of a tumor, not just detect its presence. Why is object detection insufficient here, and what does segmentation provide instead?
options: Detection provides a bounding box (a rough rectangular region), while segmentation assigns a label to every pixel, giving the exact shape and area needed for a precise measurement
Detection and segmentation produce mathematically identical outputs for this use case
Detection is always more precise than segmentation for area measurement
Segmentation cannot be applied to medical images due to resolution limits
mcqs.explanation: A bounding box only approximates an object's location with a rectangle, which is a poor proxy for irregularly-shaped structures like tumors — segmentation's per-pixel labeling gives the exact boundary needed to compute a precise area, which is exactly why segmentation, not detection, is standard in this kind of medical measurement task. The two outputs are structurally different (B is false), detection is coarser, not more precise, for this purpose (C is false), and segmentation is routinely and successfully applied to medical images (D is false).

mcqs.question: An image contains three overlapping people and a sidewalk. A team needs to count exactly how many distinct people are in the frame. Which segmentation type is necessary, and why would semantic segmentation alone fail?
options: Semantic segmentation is sufficient, since it labels every "person" pixel accurately
Instance segmentation is required, because semantic segmentation would label all three people as one undifferentiated "person" region, providing no way to count individuals
Panoptic segmentation cannot handle countable objects like people at all
Neither segmentation type can distinguish overlapping people; only object detection can
mcqs.explanation: Semantic segmentation only assigns a class label per pixel — it would correctly mark all person-pixels as "person" but has no mechanism to distinguish individual #1 from individual #2 from individual #3, making counting impossible from its output alone; instance segmentation explicitly separates individual object instances, which is exactly what's needed here. Panoptic segmentation actually does handle countable instances (alongside uncountable "stuff" regions), making C false, and object detection with reasonable box separation could approximate a count, but the question specifically asks about segmentation types, and instance segmentation is the correct answer among them (D mischaracterizes the comparison).

mcqs.question: A U-Net trained without its skip connections produces segmentation masks with blurry, imprecise object boundaries compared to the full architecture. What causes this specific failure?
options: The encoder's downsampling path discards fine spatial detail as it builds semantic understanding, and without skip connections re-injecting that detail into the decoder, the upsampled output can't recover precise boundaries
Removing skip connections has no effect on boundary precision, only on training speed
Skip connections exist only to reduce the total parameter count of the model
The decoder cannot function at all without skip connections, producing no output
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the architectural role skip connections play: the encoder's downsampling necessarily loses fine spatial detail while gaining semantic abstraction, and skip connections copy that lost detail directly across to the matching decoder stage — without them, the decoder has to reconstruct boundaries from only the heavily-downsampled bottleneck representation, producing blurrier results. This does affect output quality, not just training speed (B is false), skip connections don't reduce parameter count, they add extra connections (C is false), and the decoder still functions and produces output without them, just lower-quality output (D is false).

mcqs.question: Why is Mask R-CNN naturally suited to instance segmentation, while a standard U-Net is naturally suited to semantic segmentation instead?
options: Mask R-CNN builds on a two-stage detector, first identifying individual object regions, then predicting a mask within each — giving it an inherent per-instance structure that whole-image, per-pixel U-Net lacks
U-Net simply cannot be trained on more than one object class at a time
Mask R-CNN and U-Net use mathematically identical architectures, differing only in training data
Instance segmentation and semantic segmentation are the same task, just named differently
mcqs.explanation: Mask R-CNN's detect-then-segment design means it already has a per-object bounding region before predicting a mask, giving it a natural way to keep instances separate; U-Net operates on the whole image at once with no inherent per-object grouping, which is why it fits the class-level (semantic) framing rather than instance separation. U-Net can be trained on many classes simultaneously (B is false), the two architectures are structurally quite different, not identical (C is false), and instance vs semantic segmentation are genuinely distinct tasks with different outputs (D is false).

mcqs.question: A hospital evaluating a lesion-segmentation model chooses the Dice coefficient over pixel-wise IoU as its primary metric. What property of Dice makes it a better fit for this small-lesion use case?
options: Dice and IoU are mathematically identical, so the choice makes no difference
Dice is more sensitive to small objects relative to IoU for the same masks, which matters more when the structure of interest occupies a tiny fraction of the image, as lesions often do
Dice can only be computed for objects larger than a fixed pixel threshold
IoU cannot be computed for medical images due to their grayscale format
mcqs.explanation: Dice (2× overlap / sum of both mask sizes) is mathematically related to IoU but weights small overlaps more favorably, making it more sensitive to performance on small structures — exactly the situation with lesions or tumors that occupy a small fraction of an image, where small labeling errors matter disproportionately. Dice and IoU are related but not identical (Dice ≥ IoU for the same masks, A is false), Dice has no minimum size requirement (C is false), and IoU computation is unaffected by grayscale vs color imaging (D is false).
